title: Price distribution
question: What is the distribution of property prices?
insight: Prices range from ₹10.0 L to ₹500.0 L; median ₹254.8 L, mean ₹254.5 L, skewness +0.01. The shape is almost perfectly flat (uniform-like) (KS distance to a uniform distribution = 0.006). Real housing prices are usually strongly right-skewed, so this flat shape suggests the data is simulated rather than scraped from real listings.

title: Size distribution
question: What is the distribution of property sizes?
insight: Sizes run from 500 to 5,000 sq ft (median 2,749). The distribution is almost flat / uniform (KS distance 0.005); each size band holds a similar share of listings.

title: Price/sq ft by property type
question: How does price per sq ft vary by property type?
insight: Mean price/sq ft: highest Apartment (₹13,281), lowest Independent House (₹13,009) - a 2.1% gap. ANOVA p=0.223, effect size η²=0.0001 -> no statistically significant difference.

title: Size vs price
question: Is there a relationship between property size and price?
insight: Pearson r between size and price = +0.000 (Spearman +0.000, p=0.977): not statistically significant. Variance in price explained by size: 0.00%. Average price of homes under 1,000 sq ft is ₹255.7 L vs ₹254.8 L for 4,000-5,000 sq ft (-0.4%). Price does not rise with size, which is unusual for real markets, so size cannot be used to predict price in this dataset.

title: Outliers
question: Are there any outliers in price per sq ft or property size?
insight: IQR rule: price/sq ft has 2,808 high outliers (7.94%), while size and price have none. Outlying rows are small homes: their median size is 792 sq ft vs 2,749 overall - price/sq ft explodes because the denominator is small. They are valid combinations, so they were flagged and kept (and winsorised at the 99th percentile for modelling).

title: Price/sq ft by state
question: What is the average price per sq ft by state?
insight: Highest: Karnataka (₹13,633); lowest: Kerala (₹12,463) - a 9.4% spread. ANOVA p=0.844, η²=0.0004 -> no statistically significant difference. State explains 0.04% of the variation in price per sq ft.

title: Price by city
question: What is the average property price by city?
insight: Most expensive city: Jaipur (₹265.1 L); cheapest: Kochi (₹246.5 L) - a 7.5% gap. ANOVA p=0.911, η²=0.0008 -> no statistically significant difference. For reference, Mumbai ranks #36 and Bangalore #3 of 42 - metros are not priced above smaller cities here, unlike the real market.

title: Median age by locality
question: What is the median age of properties by locality?
insight: Across 500 localities the median age ranges 13-25 years (middle 50%: 18-20). Oldest: Locality_127 (25 yrs); newest: Locality_19 (13 yrs). Caveat: locality names (Locality_1 ... Locality_500) repeat in every city and hold ~71 listings each, so a 'locality' here is an anonymised label, not one physical neighbourhood.

title: BHK across cities
question: How is BHK distributed across cities?
insight: Overall BHK mix: 1 BHK 20.3%, 2 BHK 19.9%, 3 BHK 19.6%, 4 BHK 20.1%, 5 BHK 20.1%. Chi-square test of city vs BHK: p=0.5, Cramér's V=0.034 -> cities have the same BHK mix; any single BHK's share within a city ranges only 16%-24%.

title: Top-5 localities trend
question: What are the price trends for the top 5 most expensive localities?
insight: Top-5 localities by average price/sq ft (min 30 listings): Locality_310, Locality_123, Locality_265, Locality_133, Locality_36. The dataset has NO date column, so true price trends over time cannot be measured; the left chart shows price by construction-year cohort (price by vintage, not market movement) and shows no consistent upward or downward pattern. The right chart shows each locality's average price today vs the model's 5-year projection (assumed growth, see config.py).

title: Correlation matrix
question: How are numeric features correlated with each other?
insight: 5 pairs have |r| ≥ 0.3 (Size_in_SqFt vs Price_per_SqFt_INR; Floor_No vs Total_Floors; Price_in_Lakhs vs Price_per_SqFt_INR; Nearby_Schools vs Infrastructure_Score; Nearby_Hospitals vs Infrastructure_Score). Those are built-in: price/sq ft = price ÷ size, Infrastructure_Score is computed from schools/hospitals/transport, and Floor_No vs Total_Floors is lifted by the cleaning step that raised Total_Floors where a flat sat above the stated top floor. No strong relationship is a genuine market signal. Every other pair has |r| ≤ 0.01, i.e. size, floors, amenities and location quality are essentially uncorrelated with price.

title: Schools vs price/sq ft
question: How do nearby schools relate to price per sq ft?
insight: Pearson r between nearby schools and price/sq ft = -0.003 (Spearman -0.006, p=0.62): not statistically significant. Group means vary only 3.1% between the best (6 schools) and worst (9) group; ANOVA p=0.957 -> no statistically significant difference. More schools nearby does not translate into higher price per sq ft here.

title: Hospitals vs price/sq ft
question: How do nearby hospitals relate to price per sq ft?
insight: Pearson r between nearby hospitals and price/sq ft = -0.011 (Spearman -0.013, p=0.0443): statistically detectable but negligible. Group means vary only 5.7% between the best (3 hospitals) and worst (9) group; ANOVA p=0.383 -> no statistically significant difference.

title: Price by furnishing
question: How does price vary by furnished status?
insight: Mean price: highest Furnished (₹256.2 L), lowest Unfurnished (₹253.2 L) - 1.2% difference. ANOVA p=0.238, η²=0.00008 -> no statistically significant difference. Furnishing carries no price premium in this data.

title: Price/sq ft by facing
question: How does price per sq ft vary by property facing direction?
insight: Highest: West (₹13,277); lowest: South (₹13,043) - 1.8% gap. ANOVA p=0.598, η²=0.00005 -> no statistically significant difference. (Y-axis is truncated to make small differences visible - note how small they are.)

title: Owner types
question: How many properties belong to each owner type?
insight: Owner 11,847 | Builder 11,845 | Broker 11,667. Chi-square test against an equal split: p=0.404 -> listings are evenly split across owner types.

title: Availability status
question: How many properties are available under each availability status?
insight: Ready_to_Move: 17,721 (50.1%); Under_Construction: 17,638 (49.9%). Only two statuses exist (the brief also lists 'Sold', which is absent). Chi-square vs equal split p=0.659.

title: Parking vs price
question: Does parking space affect property price?
insight: With parking: mean price ₹254.6 L (n=17,691); without: ₹254.3 L (n=17,668) -> +0.1% difference. Welch t-test p=0.831 -> no statistically significant difference: parking does not affect price here.

title: Amenities vs price/sq ft
question: How do amenities affect price per sq ft?
insight: Pearson r between amenity count and price/sq ft = -0.015 (Spearman -0.010, p=0.00539): statistically detectable but negligible. Per-amenity differences range -2.5% to -0.9%; Playground and Pool are statistically significant at p<0.05 (with 5 tests, about 1 false positive is expected by chance); all five point slightly the opposite way to a premium (properties with the amenity are marginally cheaper per sq ft). The gaps are far too small to matter: amenities do not drive price per sq ft in this data.

title: Transport access
question: How does public transport accessibility relate to price per sq ft or investment potential?
insight: Price/sq ft: ANOVA p=0.0276, η²=0.00020 -> a statistically detectable but practically negligible difference (High ₹12,986 vs Low ₹12,974). Investment potential rises clearly with access: Good-Investment rate 8% (Low) -> 23% (Medium) -> 67% (High), and projected ROI 47.3% -> 56.6%. NOTE: that last link is by design - transport is an input to the growth assumption and the label rule - not an observed market effect.

title: Price trends by city
question: Price trends by city
insight: There is no date field, so 'price trend by city' can only be approximated by construction-year cohort. Average price by cohort moves between ₹252.1 L and ₹258.1 L (ANOVA p=0.41, η²=0.00017 -> no statistically significant difference). The right chart shows the model's 5-year projection for the priciest cities.

title: Area vs investment return
question: Correlation between area and investment return
insight: Pearson r between area and projected ROI % = +0.006 (Spearman +0.006, p=0.234): not statistically significant. Pearson r between area and absolute gain = +0.004 (Spearman +0.003, p=0.468): not statistically significant. Return *rate* is unrelated to area (growth does not depend on size in the assumption model, and price is unrelated to size in the data), so larger homes do not yield a better percentage return; absolute gain is simply driven by the price level.

title: Safety (crime proxy) vs Good Investment
question: Impact of crime rate on Good Investment classification
insight: The dataset has NO crime-rate column. Security (gated / CCTV / guard) is the closest safety proxy. Good-Investment rate: 40.4% with security vs 24.5% without (chi-square p=1.7e-223). The gap exists because security is one of the 7 criteria in the label rule (worth 1 of 9 points), so this is a built-in effect, not discovered market behaviour. To test crime impact properly, add a real crime-rate field (e.g., NCRB data by city).

title: Infrastructure vs resale value
question: Relationship between infrastructure score and resale value
insight: Infrastructure score = mean of school score, hospital score and transport score (0-1). Pearson r between infrastructure score and price/sq ft = -0.006 (Spearman -0.006, p=0.231): not statistically significant. Pearson r between infrastructure score and price = -0.003 (Spearman -0.003, p=0.562): not statistically significant. Better-served properties are not priced higher, so there is no evidence of an infrastructure premium in resale value in this data.
